Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne, Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociation: I pretend it happened to someone else, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Vignette:
Amir was twenty-seven, a physical therapist at a suburban outpatient clinic, and for three years he had been trying to hold his life together without anyone noticing the cracks. The assault happened when he was twenty-four, about a year after he married Sara. He had gone for a run in the evening along a familiar path near his old apartment. A man he did not know came up from behind, and Amir could still summon the smell of him—a sweet, musky cologne that saturated the air as the man pressed him against a fence. The rest of that evening existed in fragments: the searing pain in his shoulder as he was forced face-down, the sense of his body no longer belonging to him, the moment when something in his mind slipped sideways and he watched it all from above, telling himself this was happening to someone else. In the weeks and months afterward, Amir developed a quiet, deliberate habit of not thinking about it. Whenever the memory threatened to surface—a flash of the fence, the smell, the gravel—he would immediately turn his attention to something else: a task at work, a conversation, the television. He would mentally repeat a list of things he needed to do, or count the tiles on the ceiling, anything to keep his mind from settling on that evening. He told himself that if he did not think about it, it would not be real, and if it was not real, it could not hurt him. But the effort itself was exhausting, a constant vigilance against his own mind. And despite all his strategies, the memory would sometimes break through anyway, and then the dissociation would take over—that strange, distant calm, as though the whole thing were a story about a stranger. It allowed him to function, but he knew, deep down, that he was using these two kinds of escape—avoiding the thought, then disappearing from it—to remain absent from his own life.

At work, Amir was skilled and liked by his patients, but the clinic had become a minefield. Physical therapy required him to place his hands on people’s bodies, to guide their movements, to ask about their pain. He had learned to brace himself every time a patient mentioned a new ache. The word *pain* landed in his chest like a blow, because pain was what he felt during the assault, and now any somatic sensation—a twinge in his own back, a cramp in his leg—sent him into a silent panic. He would check and recheck his body throughout the day, pressing on his ribs, his shoulders, his lower back, scanning for anything that might signal danger or injury. He told himself it was professional vigilance, but he knew it was something else: a constant, exhausting watchfulness that left him drained by noon.

The most difficult triggers were olfactory. A middle-aged man came in for knee rehab wearing a heavy cologne, and Amir’s throat closed. He excused himself, went to the break room, and stood gripping the counter until his breathing steadied. He started avoiding certain hours when he knew that patient would be there, rearranging schedules so he would not have to be in close proximity. Another patient used a scented lotion, and Amir felt a rush of heat, a racing heart, an urge to flee. He began to dread the start of each shift, hypervigilant to the smells that drifted through the clinic. The startle responses had grown worse over time. If a patient reached out unexpectedly to touch his arm during a conversation, Amir would flinch, sometimes yanking his hand away. He could see the confusion on their faces, and he would mumble an apology, claiming he was just startled by the suddenness. Sudden movements in his peripheral vision—a colleague walking quickly past, a door swinging open—triggered the same jolt of alarm, as if his body believed danger was imminent. The world felt full of ambushes. He could not relax, even at home. Sara would come up behind him to hug him, and he would stiffen, his heart hammering. He saw the hurt in her eyes, but he could not explain it. He told himself she would not understand, and besides, he could not find the words for what had happened. He had never told her the full story.

Intimacy with Sara had become nearly impossible. Any sexual situation, even a kiss that lingered too long, brought him back to the assault. He would go distant, his mind detaching, pretending it was not his body being touched. Sara noticed his withdrawal, and she asked gently if something was wrong. He said he was just tired. He could see their marriage fraying along a seam he did not know how to mend. He felt a deep, corroding shame about his body—the body that had been used, that had not fought back, that now seemed permanently marked. He had come to believe he could never trust himself again; he had failed to protect himself that evening, and so he could not rely on his own instincts now. He also believed his emotions were broken for good. Occasionally he cried in the shower, but mostly he felt nothing—a hollowed-out numbness that scared him more than the fear did. What finally brought him to therapy was a session with a patient who had a chronic shoulder condition. The patient mentioned "the pain was so bad that night," and Amir’s mind flashed to the fence, to the gravel digging into his cheek. He dissociated mid-sentence, fumbled an exercise instruction, and walked out of the room. His supervisor noticed and expressed concern. That night, Sara told him she could not keep living with someone who was not really there. She said she loved him, but she felt alone. The next morning, Amir called a clinic that specialised in trauma. He was terrified that talking about it would shatter what little composure he had left—but he was more afraid of losing Sara, and of spending the rest of his life pretending that what happened to his body had happened to someone else.
